question: In a class, $18$ study French, $15$ study Spanish
and $8$ study both.
How many study exactly one language?

wrong.why: that counts at least one language

trap: Exactly one leaves out the middle.

beats.say: Most students get this wrong. Eighteen study French, fifteen study Spanish, and eight study both. How many study exactly one language?
Many write twenty five. Eighteen plus fifteen, minus the eight who study both.
But twenty five counts everyone who studies at least one language. Exactly one leaves out the eight in the middle.
French only is eighteen minus eight, which is ten. Spanish only is fifteen minus eight, which is seven.
Exactly one language is ten plus seven, which is seventeen.

verify:
F, S, B = 18, 15, 8
assert (F - B) + (S - B) == 17
assert F + S - B == 25          # at least one: the tempting answer
assert (F - B) + B + (S - B) == 25

youtube.description: 18 study French, 15 study Spanish, 8 study both. How many study exactly one? Not 25 — that is "at least one". Take out the middle: 10 + 7 = 17.
